questions.question: A team's strategy document lists four goals with numbers and owners, plus a themed roadmap for the quarter. Two funding requests arrive and both advance at least one goal. What is the document missing?
options: A claim about what is deciding outcomes now, which would tell you what to stop
Tighter targets, so the goals discriminate between requests
A prioritization framework applied to the two requests
Executive sign-off, so the goals carry authority
questions.explanation: Goals and a roadmap are specific about targets and dates but say nothing about why the targets are hard, so any request that touches a goal qualifies. The tempting answer is C: a prioritization framework will produce a ranking, but it will rank against the same undifferentiated goals, so the same argument recurs next month.

questions.question: Noted's PM proposes: "Our binding constraint is that enterprise team leads lose decisions after recurring meetings." What is the strongest objection?
options: Enterprise contracts are only about 20% of revenue, so the constraint is too small
Meeting summaries are an engineering problem, not a strategy problem
The claim has never been tested, and three requests through one account manager measure access to the team rather than prevalence
The constraint should be stated as a metric target so progress can be tracked
questions.explanation: The case states the underlying claim is untested and that all three requests came through one account manager within a month. That is one channel, not an independent sample. A is tempting and wrong in structure: revenue share alone neither qualifies nor disqualifies a constraint, and 20% is not small.

questions.question: You are testing three candidate constraints. What does the binding-constraint test actually require you to do?
options: Rank them by expected value and pick the highest
Assume each is fully solved tomorrow at no cost, and ask whether the outcome you care about moves
Check which one has the most supporting evidence today
Ask which one the team can deliver fastest this cycle
questions.explanation: Binding means relieving it changes the result while relieving the others does not, so you test by removing cost and delivery difficulty from the comparison. C is the tempting answer: the best-evidenced problem is often just the best-instrumented one, and evidence availability is not the same as causal weight.

questions.question: A PM concludes the binding constraint on their product is the pricing of an infrastructure provider, which another function negotiates. What does the model say to do?
options: Restate a smaller product-side problem as the binding constraint so the strategy is actionable
Drop the diagnosis and work from goals until the pricing question is resolved
Say the constraint plainly, name who controls it, then diagnose the strongest constraint inside your control
Escalate and pause product strategy work until the other function responds
questions.explanation: This is the boundary of the model: a true diagnosis can be one you cannot act on. A is the tempting failure, because the resulting document reads well and is honest-looking, but it hides the real driver from anyone who later has to explain why the strategy underperformed.

questions.question: Which statement is a diagnosis rather than a restated observation?
options: Activation fell 11% over six weeks and needs to recover to its prior level
Our activation definition is inherited and undefended, so the number is unreliable
Two changes shipped during the decline window and one of them is likely responsible
New users are not reaching a first useful document, so nothing pulls them back within the return window
questions.explanation: D proposes a mechanism a reader can disagree with and test. C is the tempting distractor: it sounds causal but only narrows the suspect list without saying what dynamic is operating, and it also assumes the cause sits inside the shipped changes.
